newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Punt/stg weakness risks Irish inflation - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Punt/stg weakness risks Irish inflation - analysts.

text.p: A sharp fall in the Irish pound's exchange rate with sterling has raised the spectre of an upsurge in inflation in Ireland's booming economy, analysts said on Monday.

"How the Irish pound is doing against sterling is always very important, not least in terms of imports with so many of our imports priced in sterling," Padraic Garvey, senior economist at Riada's Stockbrokers, said..

"It is important that the punt does not fall significantly further against sterling. The fact that the Irish pound is already weak against sterling has created inflationary dangers for Ireland," he added.

Analysts said that because Britain is Ireland's largest single trading partner, the higher costs of British imports could spark inflation in an economy growing at the fastest rate in the European Union.

Despite buoyant growth rates and strong credit growth figures, Irish inflation has remained relatively low in recent years. EU figures for September showed annualised Irish inflation running at 1.4 percent, among the lowest in the bloc.

Many economists say the punt's strength against sterling over the past year helped keep inflation low. The Irish pound broke above parity with sterling in March 1995 and climbed steadily to a high of 1.0413 sterling in August 1996.

But since then the trend has been sharply reversed. The punt fell 1.3 percent against sterling in September and 2.4 percent in October. At the same time, it appreciated against the mark, hitting three-year highs last week and climbing to the top of the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) grid.
Davy Stockbrokers said this situation posed a dilemma for the central bank's exchange rate policy -- should it try to track sterling or the mark?

"Close tracking of sterling may impinge upon the exchange rate eligibility criteria for EMU that a currency be within the 2.25 percent ERM bands for at least two years prior to the start of the system in 1999," Davy said.

"On the other hand, if the punt tracks the mark then the sterling/Irish rate will fall and there is an overwhelming body of evidence that suggests that this feeds through to price inflation, and does so relatively quickly," it added.

Davy said this could result in Ireland missing the Maastricht criteria under the requirement for the 1997 inflation rate to be no more than 1.5 percent above the average of the three lowest inflation rates in the system.

Alan McQuaid, economist at Bloxham Stockbrokers, said that while the central bank was concerned with import prices, it seemed more worried about house prices and credit growth. He predicted an interest rate rise to ease the risk of inflation.
"If your main worry is domestic housing prices and domestic credit growth then the only way to counter that is to have higher interest rates," McQuaid said.
"The central bank is probably looking towards a rate rise in the short-term which will push the Irish pound back up against sterling," he added.
But Eunan King at NCB Stockbrokers said there was no need for a rate rise as he believed there was no inflationary threat in Ireland at all.
"The most important thing to focus on is the trade-weighted index here which was up half a percent on the week. That is roughly three percent up on the average of last year," he said.

"I think when you look at the econometric studies that have been done on Irish inflation going back over the last 20 years, they have concluded that it is inflation in our trading partners and the exchange rate measured by the trade-weighted index that are the two most important determants," King added.
